This paper tackles an important and timely problem: standard NLI benchmarks such as SNLI and MultiNLI are known to contain annotation artifacts and shallow shortcuts, so raw test accuracy often overstates genuine inference ability. The paper proposes an automated way to derive a harder evaluation subset from an existing test set by clustering examples according to training-dynamics features. The method extends dataset cartography by combining confidence, variability, correctness, and AUM, computed under both full-input and hypothesis-only training, and then fitting a GMM to partition examples into easy, ambiguous, and hard groups. The paper further applies the same characterization to training data and argues that substantial data reduction is possible without hurting robustness, sometimes improving performance on stress tests.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and potentially useful. The central idea is intuitive: examples that are easy to fit even in a hypothesis-only setting are likely to reflect artifacts, while examples that remain difficult under full-input training may better probe actual reasoning. The empirical trends are also broadly plausible. In particular, the monotonic drop in performance from easy to hard splits, and the collapse of hypothesis-only accuracy on the hard split, are both consistent with the intended interpretation. The attempt to move beyond manually constructed stress tests toward automatically mined “naturally hard” subsets is a worthwhile contribution.

That said, I have substantial concerns about the methodology and the strength of the claims. The biggest issue is that the proposed test-set characterization is obtained by training directly on the test set itself. The authors note that this is done “only to gather training dynamics,” but this does not remove the conceptual problem: the hardness labels are defined by memorization behavior on the evaluation set under supervised access to its gold labels. This makes the resulting split less of an independently derived benchmark and more of a post hoc partition based on how easily a particular model family can fit those labeled examples. Such a procedure may still be useful for dataset analysis, but it weakens the claim that the method constructs a generally valid “strong test set” for model evaluation. At minimum, the paper should more clearly frame the contribution as diagnostic characterization rather than benchmark construction, unless it can show that the same hardness partition can be predicted without label access on the test set.

Relatedly, the claim of model-agnosticism is only partially supported. The cross-model transfer experiment between RoBERTa and DeBERTa is a good start, but both are closely related pretrained transformer encoders fine-tuned in nearly identical ways. This is not enough to establish model independence in a strong sense. More importantly, Table 4 actually suggests notable discrepancies across source models, especially for ambiguous and hard splits in MultiNLI, where accuracies differ substantially depending on which model induced the partition. That does not invalidate the approach, but it suggests the partition is at least somewhat model-relative. The paper should temper the “model-agnostic” claim and quantify agreement directly, for example with adjusted Rand index, NMI, or overlap percentages between partitions induced by different models and random seeds.

A second major concern is whether the method is genuinely discovering “difficulty” rather than mostly rediscovering label imbalance and known dataset biases. The hard splits in SNLI and MultiNLI contain many more neutral examples, while easy splits contain more entailment and contradiction. Since neutral is often the hardest class in these datasets, a large part of the observed accuracy drop may simply reflect class composition rather than a deeper notion of difficulty. The paper acknowledges this distribution shift, but does not control for it. A stronger analysis would report per-class accuracy within each difficulty split, or construct class-balanced easy/ambiguous/hard subsets. Without such controls, it is difficult to know how much of the effect comes from reduced artifacts versus changed label priors.

The statistical analysis of spurious correlations is also weaker than the paper suggests. The heuristics used—word overlap, antonyms, length mismatch, misspellings, negation—are reasonable but limited proxies. Showing that these heuristics become less class-differentiated in the hard split is suggestive, but not sufficient to conclude that spurious correlations have been “minimized” or that the resulting set is more realistic. Some artifacts in NLI are much subtler and lexicalized in ways these heuristics will not capture. Moreover, the Mann-Whitney tests compare heuristic distributions across labels, but the paper does not clearly specify the exact hypotheses tested, effect sizes, or the number of comparisons corrected by Bonferroni. Statistical significance alone is not very informative here, especially with large sample sizes. Reporting effect sizes and confidence intervals would make the argument more convincing.

There are also some technical and presentation issues that need attention. The formula for variability appears incorrect: the standard deviation should involve squared deviations, but Equation (2) omits the square. The correctness equation is also malformed typographically. These may be typesetting mistakes, but they matter because the method depends directly on these features. The description of the clustering is somewhat under-specified as well. Why exactly three clusters? Is this fixed to mimic Data Maps, or supported by model selection criteria such as BIC/AIC? Since the authors motivate GMM as a more flexible alternative to thresholding, it would be natural to justify the number of components empirically. Similarly, the covariance type, initialization, and sensitivity to random seeds are not discussed. Because clustering can be unstable, especially in low dimensions with correlated features, robustness analysis is important.

The training-set characterization results are promising but also somewhat hard to interpret. The paper compares against Data Maps and AUM, but the baselines are adapted in somewhat ad hoc ways. For example, selecting “ambiguous” examples via top variability percentiles is standard for Data Maps, but the exact thresholding and the mapping to the authors’ cluster combinations may not be fully comparable. Likewise, the AUM baseline uses percentile ranges that are not part of the original method. Since the proposed method uses eight features and a learned clustering model, while the baselines are reduced to simple threshold rules, the comparison may favor the proposed approach by construction. A fairer comparison would include stronger baselines such as supervised artifact detectors, confidence-based filtering using only full-input dynamics, or clustering on the original cartography features with the same GMM. An ablation study would also be very valuable: how much do the gains come from adding hypothesis-only dynamics, from adding AUM, or from replacing thresholding with GMM?

I also think the paper overstates the realism of the resulting hard split. The authors argue that because the examples come from the original dataset rather than being manually or adversarially constructed, they are more natural. That is plausible, but “natural” does not necessarily mean “better evaluation.” If the hard split is enriched for annotation ambiguity, rare phenomena, or even mislabeled examples, then lower accuracy may not reflect better reasoning evaluation. The FEVER results are especially interesting here: the hard split becomes extremely difficult, but the paper itself notes that FEVER has fewer hypothesis-only artifacts, suggesting the method may be capturing generic difficulty rather than artifact reduction. This is not a flaw, but it means the interpretation of the hard split differs across datasets. The paper should separate these two notions more carefully: artifact-poor versus intrinsically difficult.

Another concern is practical usefulness. If constructing the split requires training two supervised models on the labeled test set for multiple epochs, then the method is expensive and awkward for benchmark design. It may still be acceptable as a one-time offline analysis tool, but then the contribution is closer to dataset auditing than benchmark creation. The paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of the intended deployment scenario. For example: is the goal that benchmark creators release these hardness annotations once, and future model developers evaluate on them? If so, how stable are the annotations across architectures and seeds? If instead each practitioner is expected to recompute them, then the method is much less practical.

Despite these concerns, there are several strengths worth highlighting. The paper addresses a real problem and does so with a conceptually coherent approach. The use of hypothesis-only dynamics as part of the feature representation is a nice idea and probably the most novel aspect of the work. The experiments span SNLI, MultiNLI, and FEVER, which helps show some breadth. The training-set filtering results suggest the method may have utility beyond evaluation, and the qualitative examples are helpful in building intuition. I also appreciate that the authors compare against both Data Maps and AUM rather than only presenting absolute results.

To strengthen the paper, I would strongly encourage the following revisions or additional experiments. First, provide ablations: full-input dynamics only versus adding hypothesis-only dynamics; confidence/variability/correctness only versus adding AUM; GMM versus simple thresholding on the same feature set. Second, quantify stability across random seeds and across models, including direct partition agreement metrics. Third, control for label imbalance by reporting class-balanced results or per-class accuracies within each split. Fourth, justify the choice of three clusters, ideally with model selection criteria and perhaps results for alternative numbers of clusters. Fifth, clarify the statistical testing setup and report effect sizes. Sixth, fix the equations and improve the exposition around the exact training protocol. Finally, and most importantly, temper the claims around “constructing a strong test set” unless the authors can address the concern that the split is induced using supervised access to the test labels themselves.

My overall assessment is that this is a promising paper with an interesting idea, but the current version does not yet fully support its strongest claims. I would describe it as a useful dataset analysis method with potential for benchmark curation, rather than a definitive solution for automated stress-test construction. With stronger methodological validation and more careful framing, it could become a solid contribution.

If I were making a recommendation, it would be borderline leaning negative in its current form, mainly because of the test-set-on-test-set training issue and the insufficient evidence for model-agnostic, artifact-minimizing benchmark construction. However, I do think the core idea is worthwhile, and I would encourage the authors to revise and resubmit with a tighter empirical case and more restrained claims.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes an automated method to characterize NLI datasets into easy/ambiguous/hard subsets using training-dynamics features. For each test example, the authors train models directly on the test split in two settings—premise+hypothesis and hypothesis-only—and extract eight features (confidence, variability, correctness, AUM in both settings). A Gaussian Mixture Model clusters examples into three difficulty levels, which are then interpreted as a harder stress-test-like partition. Experiments on SNLI, MultiNLI, and FEVER show monotonic performance degradation from easy to hard, reduced hypothesis-only accuracy on hard subsets, and weaker heuristic artifact signals on hard subsets. The same characterization is also applied to training data, where selected subsets reportedly match or exceed full-data performance on Naik et al.'s stress tests while using less data.
strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: standard NLI benchmarks contain annotation artifacts and inflated performance due to spurious correlations.
The proposed approach is simple, largely model-agnostic in implementation, and leverages existing data rather than manually constructing adversarial examples.
Uses multiple training-dynamics features and combines premise+hypothesis with hypothesis-only signals, which is a reasonable extension over standard dataset cartography.
Empirical results show clear monotonic degradation across easy/ambiguous/hard splits on several datasets, suggesting the clustering captures some notion of difficulty.
Includes cross-model comparison with RoBERTa and DeBERTa and an exploratory application to training-set filtering.
The paper attempts statistical analysis of heuristic artifact measures across splits and labels rather than relying only on anecdotal examples.
weaknesses: The central methodology trains models on the test set to characterize the test set, which is highly unconventional and undermines the validity of the resulting benchmark as an evaluation protocol.

The paper conflates memorization/learnability under direct supervision on the target split with intrinsic example difficulty; examples that are hard to fit in 5 epochs are not necessarily better indicators of robust generalization.
There is no convincing evidence that the hard split is a superior benchmark for model comparison rather than simply a subset with more neutral labels or lower lexical regularity.
The claim of reduced spurious correlations is supported only by a small set of shallow heuristics; absence of significance on these heuristics does not imply absence of artifacts.
The method requires labels for the test set and repeated supervised training on it, making it impractical for standard benchmark construction and potentially circular as an evaluation methodology.
The cross-model generalization evidence is mixed: some source-target split transfers show large discrepancies, especially for ambiguous/hard MultiNLI and FEVER, weakening the model-agnostic claim.
The training-set filtering experiments are difficult to interpret because gains are measured on Naik et al.'s stress tests, which the paper itself argues are artificial and mismatched to its goals.
Presentation quality is uneven, with grammatical issues and several unclear or inconsistent descriptions (e.g., number of clusters, split naming, and some table formatting).
methodological_flaws: A major scientific-logic issue is the use of the test set itself as supervised training data to derive the benchmark partition. This leaks label information into benchmark construction and makes the resulting 'hard test set' dependent on fitting dynamics on the very examples later used for evaluation.

Equation (2) for variability appears mathematically incorrect: the variance term omits squaring, i.e., it uses sum(p-mean) rather than sum((p-mean)^2). If this is not a typographical error, the feature is invalid; if it is, the paper should clarify implementation versus manuscript formula.
The correctness equation is malformed/incomplete in notation, making it unclear whether the indicator is computed correctly. Such notation issues matter because these features drive the clustering.
The paper states clustering into three clusters, but earlier text says 'three difficulty levels (4 for P+H and four for H)', which is inconsistent and raises concerns about methodological clarity.

Ranking clusters solely by average confidence from the P+H model imposes the desired ordering post hoc and may bias interpretation; no intrinsic validation of the GMM structure or number of clusters is provided (e.g., BIC/AIC, stability across seeds, alternative cluster counts).

Empirical validity is limited because there are no baselines that characterize test difficulty without training on the test set, such as using training-derived dynamics, held-out predictors of hardness, or unsupervised lexical/semantic difficulty measures.

The statistical claim 'no evidence for spurious correlations in the hard split' is too strong: failing to reject differences on a few heuristics via Mann-Whitney tests does not establish artifact removal, especially after multiple dependent comparisons and with potentially reduced sample sizes.

The training-set filtering comparison may be unfair or under-specified: Data Maps and AUM are reduced to percentile heuristics, while the proposed method uses richer features and hypothesis-only models; hyperparameter parity and seed variance are not reported.

No uncertainty estimates or multi-seed variance are reported for the main benchmarking results, despite clustering and fine-tuning instability potentially affecting split composition and downstream accuracies.

Because hard splits contain substantially different label distributions (notably more neutral examples), part of the observed accuracy drop may be due to class-composition shift rather than genuine robustness difficulty; this confound is acknowledged descriptively but not controlled experimentally.
